characters: No characters: each page is a colour picture of something in Ghana (sun, stars, cocoa leaf, sea, night drums, white clouds and a kente cloth).

narrationPlan.voice: Bright, sing-song voice, like a nursery teacher leading a class
narrationPlan.pace: Bouncy and clear, with a clap on every rhyme (about 70 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Light marimba with a skipping rhythm (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Kente is a hand-woven cloth from Ghana. The poem uses colours from nature and does not give the traditional meanings of kente colours, which vary and are best learned from weavers and elders.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check that every line is simple enough for ages 3 to 5 and that the rhymes (sky/high, tree/sea, still/hill, strip/tip) are clear in Ghanaian English.

teacherGuide.overview: A first rhyme. Children hear pairs of rhyming words, name colours and link them to things they see in Ghana. Form: four couplets (rhyme scheme AA BB CC DD).
learningGoals: Say a short poem by heart.
beforeReading: Show a piece of kente or a picture of one.
afterReading: Weave paper strips of the six colours into a mat.
Find objects in the room for each colour.
discussion: Which two words rhyme in each pair?

mathsExtension.task: The rhyme names six colours. Count them.
mathsExtension.answer: Red, gold, green, blue, black and white make 6.

support: Say one line at a time and let children echo.
stretch: Make a new couplet about a seventh colour.

culturalNotes: Kente is a hand-woven cloth from Ghana. The poem uses colours from nature and does not give the traditional meanings of kente colours, which vary and are best learned from weavers and elders.
localiseThis: Invite a weaver or elder to talk about kente.
Do not tell children what each colour “means” unless an elder or weaver has shared it.
